source.title: Deep models reveal better strategies for superposition

record.file_problem: The full post is present, but web rendering omits some equations, symbols, and numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests sparse-feature superposition in a 4-feature, 2D toy network and argues from its own results that uniform geometries are not inherently optimal: deeper decoders learn asymmetric and sometimes opened feature pairs.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on toy-network feature geometry and reconstruction. Prior-work results are not counted. Several numerical values in the post's prose and captions are missing in the web rendering.
record.test_reason: It trains 4-feature to 2D toy networks: a tied ReLU and 1–4 bilinear decoder layers, 20 runs each. It classifies the learned superposition geometry and argues that uniform geometry is an artifact of shallow decoders. This bears directly on V1's 'regular geometry' element.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that uniform polytopes are not inherently optimal for equal-importance, equal-sparsity features. Symmetric antipodal pairs arise from shallow decoders (tied ReLU, one bilinear layer), while deeper decoders use asymmetry and tilting to reduce error. They attribute this to decoder expressivity and leave open whether it carries over to real networks.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a linear encoder followed by one or more bilinear MLPs, with a 4-feature-to-2D bottleneck and reconstruction MSE. The original study used two-layer ReLU networks with tied weights. This post directly compares a tied-ReLU case but mainly investigates a different, deeper decoder family.
record.method_sensitivity: The learned geometry changes with decoder depth. The best opening and the cost of shortening embeddings depend on binned-decoder resolution.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark decoders show that asymmetric and slightly opened antipodal pairs reach lower reconstruction MSE than closed symmetric pairs. The optimal opening and length ratio depend on decoder resolution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For equal-importance, equal-sparsity features, uniform or symmetric superposition geometries are not the theoretical MSE optimum. Lower-loss asymmetric geometries exist that only sufficiently expressive decoders can exploit.

record.problems: Evidence is from a single toy setup with 4 features and a 2D bottleneck; the study does not test higher-dimensional bottlenecks or LLMs. Geometry categories summarize 20 runs per architecture, and the post reports no uncertainty estimates. Some numerical values and equations are missing in the web rendering.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; all extracted rows are included.

untested.parts: Sparsity-dependent phase transition (sparsity fixed); varying importance; more features or higher-dimensional bottlenecks; near-orthogonality beyond the 2D antipodal case.

missing.what: Trained-model versus best-in-class decoder MSE (1 bilinear: 0.0093 vs 0.0093, 0% gap; 4 bilinear: 0.0060 vs 0.0041, 31.9% gap, saturating near 18%). This is context for whether deep models reach the asymmetric optimum.

record.verdict_notes: Rows R6–R8 are theoretical benchmark computations, so I unlinked them from V1 and recorded them as fits_no_version. I used limits_scope rather than challenges for the deep models, because superposition itself persists and only the regularity component fails, conditional on architecture. The setting is a single 4-to-2D configuration at one sparsity, with no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: The study fixes a 4-feature, 2D bottleneck setup with sparse, equally important features; it does not sweep feature sparsity, importance, feature count, or bottleneck dimension. Its results concern this architecture and task.
It does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by competition for limited capacity, or whether more important features receive dedicated dimensions.
It does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
It does not study LLM activations, feature spreading across neurons, or SAE recovery.
It does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
It represents each input feature by an encoder vector, but does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: linear encoder with unrestricted binned decoder
rows.operation_detail: Searched encoder geometries using random search followed by local descent, scoring with a binned decoder.

conditions.value: two-dimensional bins; resolution stated as bins in the text, but the numerical value is missing in the web rendering
four parameters; random search followed by local descent

rows.baseline: Closed symmetric pairs decoded at the same resolution; numerical MSE is missing in the web rendering.
rows.value: The search found two asymmetric, slightly opened pairs; the free embeddings were much shorter than the pinned embeddings. The post reports lower MSE than for closed symmetric pairs, but the numerical values are missing in the web rendering.
rows.locator: Section 3.4, search for the best strategy
rows.note: The article describes each short embedding as tilted toward the long embedding of the other pair.
rows.check: This is the authors' own benchmark: a hand-optimized encoder scored by a binned decoder, not a trained network. It is a theoretical-optimum result, not a measure of what networks learn. Values are missing in the rendering.

rows.subject: linear encoder with binned decoder
rows.operation_detail: Swept the opening angle of one feature pair and scored with binned decoders.

conditions.value: three; exact bin counts are missing in the web rendering

rows.measure: Reconstruction MSE as a function of pair opening
rows.baseline: Closed pair; numerical MSE is missing in the web rendering.
rows.value: MSE had a minimum at a finite opening; the minimizing opening moved toward zero as bins became finer.
rows.locator: Section 3.3, binned-decoder opening-angle figure and accompanying text
rows.note: The post attributes the finite-resolution optimum and subsequent interference to the opened pair interacting with readings of the other pair.
rows.check: This is an analytic sweep over hand-set encoder geometries with binned decoders, not trained-model behaviour. It supports the authors' argument but is not a V1 observation.

rows.subject: linear encoder with binned decoder
rows.operation_detail: Swept the length ratio of a closed antipodal pair and computed the best-decoder MSE.
rows.measure: Summed MSE of the two features as a function of embedding-length ratio
rows.baseline: Symmetric pair; numerical MSE and exact minimizing ratios are missing in the web rendering.
rows.value: Moderate asymmetry reduced summed MSE; the curve flattened near its minimum and rose again at larger ratios. Binned decoders also had a minimum at the same ratio, with coarser bins becoming worse sooner beyond it.
rows.locator: Section 3.2, asymmetry sweep and accompanying text
rows.note: The post says the optimum is shallow and that excessive shortening makes the short feature unreadable when its partner is active.
rows.check: This is a closed-form or binned benchmark sweep of the length ratio on a fixed pair, not trained-model behaviour. Numbers are missing in the rendering.

relation.reason: The study trains toy reconstruction networks and measures their learned superposition geometry directly.

tranche.reason: The depth sweep and decoder analysis argue that V1's regular geometry requires qualification by decoder expressivity.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. Geometry is measured at fixed sparsity and equal importance; joint sparsity-by-importance coverage and transfer to real networks remain untested. Missing mathematical expressions do not affect the checked table.

reader_labels.condition: tied ReLU and one bilinear layer
reader_labels.reason: Most runs in both shallow settings had symmetric antipodal pairs, matching the regular-pair geometry in this tested setup; one run in each setting was categorized as other (R1, R2).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: two, three, and four bilinear layers
reader_labels.reason: The deeper networks commonly learned asymmetric pairs, and most three-layer runs and half of four-layer runs also opened pairs; the study argues uniform geometry is not inherently optimal (R3, R4, R5, R6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The benefits and chosen geometry depended on decoder resolution: the best finite opening shifted toward zero with finer bins, and excess asymmetry or opening could worsen reconstruction (R7, R8).
